Pipelines

A pipeline is the core unit of work in Godzilla: a named, versioned data-processing workflow that moves data from a source connector, through zero or more transform steps, to a destination connector. Every pipeline runs as a sequence of events flowing through that path.

Anatomy of a pipeline

Every pipeline has three parts:

  • Source — the connector that emits events into the pipeline (a database, a queue, an upload, a webhook).
  • Transforms — an ordered list of steps that reshape, filter, or enrich events as they pass through. Transforms are optional; a pipeline with none is a pass-through copy.
  • Destination — the connector that events are written to once transforms complete.
Pipelines are declarative

You describe the desired source, transforms, and destination; Godzilla schedules and retries the runs. You never manage worker processes directly.

Pipeline state

A pipeline is always in one of three states:

  • draft — configured but not yet processing events.
  • active — running on its configured schedule or trigger.
  • paused — temporarily stopped; resumes from the last checkpoint.

Versioning

Pipeline configuration is versioned. Publishing a new version does not affect events already in flight on the previous version — in-flight runs finish on the version they started on. This matters most when a pipeline definition is part of a larger migration; see the Migration guide for an example of retiring an old pipeline version safely.

Godzilla distinguishes two kinds of events:

Ordering

Events are delivered in-order per source partition, not globally. Two events from different source partitions may be processed out of order relative to each other.

Every event carries a payload — the actual user data. To ensure payload consistency and enable validation, you declare the expected shape of a payload using a schema. Schemas let connectors validate incoming data and allow transform code to safely access fields with IDE autocomplete.

Schemas

A schema is a declaration of the shape and types of fields in an event payload. Schemas ensure data consistency as events flow through your pipelines, allow destinations to validate incoming data, and power IDE autocomplete and validation in transforms.

Why schemas matter

Without explicit schemas, a pipeline has no way to know whether an incoming event's payload matches what the destination expects. Schemas solve this by:

  • Validating — Rejecting events that don't match the declared shape before they reach a destination.
  • Documenting — Making it clear to other engineers what fields a pipeline carries and what types they have.
  • Enabling safety checks — Detecting schema drift (unplanned changes to event shape) as data sources evolve.
  • Powering transforms — In transform code, your IDE can autocomplete fields because it knows the schema.

Declaring a schema

Schemas are declared at the connector level, not at the pipeline level. A source connector declares the shape of events it emits; a destination connector declares the shape it expects to receive.

{

Error handling & recovery

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

pipeline-retry-config.json json 
{
  "retry_policy": {
    "max_attempts": 5,
    "backoff": "exponential",
    "initial_delay_ms": 1000
  }
}

Dead-lettering

Transforming events in flight

Once you've connected a data source, events flow through your pipeline as structured data. This guide covers how to reshape, filter, and enrich those events before they reach their destination.

Overview

Transformations apply at the pipeline level and run on every event that enters the pipeline. You can:

  • Reshape — flatten nested objects, rename fields, or project a subset of columns
  • Filter — discard events matching certain criteria (e.g., test events, low-value rows)
  • Enrich — add new fields by joining external data or deriving values from existing fields

Reshaping events

The most common transformation is projecting fields — keeping only the columns you need and renaming them for the destination system.

transform-project.json json 
{
  "transform": {
    "type": "project",
    "fields": {
      "user_id": "id",
      "user_email": "email",
      "user_created_at": "created_at"
    }
  }
}

This transformation reads the id, email, and created_at fields from incoming events and emits them as user_id, user_email, and user_created_at. Any other fields are dropped.

Flattening nested objects

Use dot notation in field names to flatten nested objects: "address.city" becomes a top-level city field, or map it to any name you prefer.

Filtering events

Filter transforms discard events matching a predicate, reducing noise and cost by not storing or processing unwanted data.

transform-filter.json json 
{
  "transform": {
    "type": "filter",
    "condition": {
      "field": "status",
      "operator": "!=",
      "value": "test"
    }
  }
}

This filter drops all events where the status field is test. Only events with a non-test status are passed to the destination. Filtered events do not incur downstream costs and do not appear in the dead-letter queue.

Enriching events

Enrichment adds new fields to events by consulting an external source — a dimension table, a cache, or a derived calculation.

transform-enrich.json json 
{
  "transform": {
    "type": "enrich",
    "lookups": {
      "customer_tier": {
        "source": "dimension_customers",
        "match_on": "customer_id",
        "select": "tier"
      }
    }
  }
}

This enrichment joins the incoming customer_id against a dimension table called dimension_customers, looks up the tier column, and adds it as a new field on every event.

Enrichment latency

External lookups add latency to each event. Keep dimension tables small and indexed on the join key. For high-volume pipelines, consider caching or materializing the lookup data closer to the pipeline.

Combining transformations

You can chain multiple transforms in a single pipeline — they run left to right. A common pattern is filter first (drop unwanted rows early), then project, then enrich.

pipeline-multi-transform.json json 
{
  "pipeline_id": "enrich-and-filter-orders",
  "transforms": [
    { "type": "filter", "condition": { "field": "amount", "operator": ">", "value": 0 } },
    { "type": "project", "fields": { "order_id": "id", "order_amount": "amount", "customer_id": "cust_id" } },
    { "type": "enrich", "lookups": { "customer_tier": { "source": "dimension_customers", "match_on": "customer_id", "select": "tier" } } }
  ]
}

Performance and debugging

Check the pipeline's transform metrics in the monitoring dashboard (see Monitoring & alerts) to watch transform latency and filter drop rates. If transforms are too slow or your enrichment lookups time out, you'll see pipeline events queue up — review and optimize the transform definition.

Backfill historical data

When building a new pipeline to a destination system, you often need to load historical data from your source in addition to new events flowing forward. This recipe shows how to backfill data alongside live event streaming.

Overview

Backfilling typically involves:

  1. Setting up your connectors and pipeline for live event streaming
  2. Running a separate backfill process to pull historical records
  3. Ensuring the backfill and live pipeline don't duplicate events

Setting up the pipeline

First, create your source and destination connectors and activate the pipeline to start processing new events:

setup-pipeline.sh bash 
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "orders-to-warehouse",
    "source_connector_id": "conn_postgres_orders",
    "destination_connector_id": "conn_snowflake_warehouse"
  }'

Running the backfill

Use your source system's native tools to extract historical data and replay it through the pipeline. For example, with Postgres:

backfill.sh bash 
psql -h orders-db.example.com -U user -d orders_db -c \
  "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at < NOW() - interval '30 days'" | \
  curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \

To prevent events from appearing twice in your destination:

Use an event timestamp cutoff

Fan-out to multiple destinations

A common architecture pattern is to stream events from a single source system to multiple destinations. This recipe shows how to set up parallel pipelines so events reach warehouses, real-time analytics platforms, and operational databases simultaneously.

Overview

Fan-out workflows let you:

  • Maintain a single source of truth while serving multiple downstream systems
  • Process the same events through different transforms for each destination
  • Decouple destination failures from affecting other pipelines

Creating multiple pipelines

Create a separate pipeline for each destination, all reading from the same source connector:

create-pipelines.sh bash 
# Pipeline 1: to data warehouse
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "events-to-warehouse",
    "source_connector_id": "conn_kafka_events",
    "destination_connector_id": "conn_snowflake_warehouse"
  }'

# Pipeline 2: to real-time analytics
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "events-to-analytics",
    "source_connector_id": "conn_kafka_events",
    "destination_connector_id": "conn_mixpanel_analytics"
  }'

# Pipeline 3: to operational database
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "events-to-operational-db",
    "source_connector_id": "conn_kafka_events",
    "destination_connector_id": "conn_postgres_operational"
  }'

Transforming for each destination

Each pipeline can apply destination-specific transforms without affecting others. For example, reshape the event schema for your warehouse while filtering sensitive fields for analytics:

{
  "transform_type": "jq",

Isolated failures

Events retry only in the failed pipeline; other pipelines continue delivering to their destinations. Use the Events API to monitor each pipeline's delivery status independently.

  echo "=== $pipeline ==="

    -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \

Fan-out to multiple destinations

A common architecture pattern is to stream events from a single source system to multiple destinations. This recipe shows how to set up parallel pipelines so events reach warehouses, real-time analytics platforms, and operational databases simultaneously.

Overview

Fan-out workflows let you:

  • Maintain a single source of truth while serving multiple downstream systems
  • Process the same events through different transforms for each destination
  • Decouple destination failures from affecting other pipelines

Creating multiple pipelines

Create a separate pipeline for each destination, all reading from the same source connector:

create-pipelines.sh bash 
# Pipeline 1: to data warehouse
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "events-to-warehouse",
    "source_connector_id": "conn_kafka_events",
    "destination_connector_id": "conn_snowflake_warehouse"
  }'

# Pipeline 2: to real-time analytics
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "events-to-analytics",
    "source_connector_id": "conn_kafka_events",
    "destination_connector_id": "conn_mixpanel_analytics"
  }'

# Pipeline 3: to operational database
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "events-to-operational-db",
    "source_connector_id": "conn_kafka_events",
    "destination_connector_id": "conn_postgres_operational"
  }'

Transforming for each destination

Each pipeline can apply destination-specific transforms without affecting others. For example, reshape the event schema for your warehouse while filtering sensitive fields for analytics:

transform-for-warehouse.json json 
{
  "transform_type": "jq",
  "script": ". | {event_id, user_id, timestamp, event_type, properties: .properties | del(.internal_notes, .cost)}"
}

Error handling

Each pipeline has independent error and retry policies. If one destination fails:

Isolated failures

Events retry only in the failed pipeline; other pipelines continue delivering to their destinations. Use the Events API to monitor each pipeline's delivery status independently.

Monitoring fan-out pipelines

Check delivery status across all destination pipelines:

monitor-pipelines.sh bash 
for pipeline in "events-to-warehouse" "events-to-analytics" "events-to-operational-db"; do
  echo "=== $pipeline ==="
  curl https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
    -d "{\"pipeline_id\": \"$pipeline\", \"status\": \"delivered\"}"
done
